Park and Charles F. Gower Abstract: A paleomagnetic study of mafic plutonic rocks in the northeast Grenville Province found five magnetizations, interpreted as Grenvillian and later overprints. Components A, B, and C, with the highest unblocking temperatures and distinct regional distributions, have paleopoles that appear to lie on the Grenville Track. Component C, with pole at 34S0E, 11"s (6p, 6m = 2", 4") and mostly distributed in lower-grade mafic rocks in the Groswater Bay terrane near the Grenville Front, is interpreted as a post ca. 970 Ma Grenville overprint, predating components A and B. The latter components, nearly coextensive in distribution in the Groswater Bay and Sandwich Bay regions farther south, have respective poles at 326"E, 02"N (N = 9 sites; 6p, 6m = So, 11 ") and 34S0E, 13"N (N = 13 sites; 6p, 6m = 6", 8"). Component B could be interpreted either as a Grenville overp

or the other suite. As a result, primary olivine - clinopyroxene - plagioclase - biotite -opaque mineral assemblages (typical of the Michael gabbro) are replaced, first by garnet- and orthopyroxene-bearing coronitic-textured metagabbros and ultimately by two-pyroxene f garnet granu- lites. In this paper we report on magnetostratigraphic dating and correlation of three sections recording Late Pliocene to Late Pleistocene glaciations: Katherine Creek, Little Bear River, and Inlin Brook (located around 6S0N, 127"W). Each section consists of a colluvial unit overlying a Pliocene pediment surface cut into Proterozoic or Paleozoic bedrock, or Tertiary gravel, which is in turn overlain by a stack of five, and in places six, montane tills, usually with soils developed at their surfaces, and capped by a Laurentide till. Normal and reversed magnetizations were recognized with single-domain magnetite as a dominant remanence carrier. Introduction Late Cenozoic magnetostratigraphy has over the past 30 years been a very useful tool for the correlation and dating of terrestrial geologic deposits, and as such has served to establish time lines in sedimentary sequences, which contain proxy records of past climates (e.g., Birkeland et al. 1980; Easterbrook and Boellstorff 1982; Barendregt and Vincent 1990). Sedimentary deposits in the range of 1 - 3 Ma offer few other possibilities for absolute dating. Where suitable fine-grained sediments exist, their paleomagnetic polarity can be determined and, using ancillary information, corre- lated with the geomagnetic polarity time scale. Such deposits may be assigned to the Late Pliocene and Early Pleistocene (Matuyama reversed polarity chron: 2.6-0.78 Ma) or Late Pleistocene (Brunhes normal polarity chron: < 0.78 Ma), or to one of the magnetic polarity subchrons within the Matuvama Chron. ~6e Late Cenozoic sedimentary record of the northern Canadian Cordillera is extensive and contains evidence of several glacial and interglacial periods. The purpose of this study was to establish the suitability of the tills and associated paleosols for paleomag- netic analysis and to attempt a correlation of these deposits with the reference Quaternary magnetostratigraphic time scale. In this paper we report on magnetostratigraphic dating and correlation of three sections recording Late Pliocene to Late Pleistocene glaciations: Katherine Creek, Little Bear River, and Inlin Brook (located around 6S0N, 127"W). Each section consists of a colluvial unit overlying a Pliocene pediment surface cut into Proterozoic or Paleozoic bedrock, or Tertiary gravel, which is in turn overlain by a stack of five, and in places six, montane tills, usually with soils developed at their surfaces, and capped by a Laurentide till. Normal and reversed magnetizations were recognized with single-domain magnetite as a dominant remanence carrier. The Katherine Creek section has a normally magnetized colluvium at its base, which is overlain by two reversed tills, succeeded by three normal tills. We interpret the top two tills to be of Brunhes age (<780 ka) but argue that the lowermost normal till is of probable Olduvai age (ca. 1.8 Ma). The two underlying tills are of Matuyama age (2.6 Ma to 780 ka), and the colluvial base is assigned to the Gauss (3.5-2.6 Ma). The Little Bear River section exposes a stratigraphic record similar to that found at Katherine Creek. Only four units could be assigned a paleornagnetic polarity, the others yielding incoherent results. Paleosol

Petrography and geochemistry Marathon dykes are quartz tholeiites that consist largely of equigranular to subophitic clinopyroxene and plagioclase in approximately equal proportions. Lesser amounts of amphi- Me, magnetite, myrmekite, quartz, biotite, and apatite, in approximate order of decreasing abundance, have an aggre- gate modal content of about 10 - 15 76. The pyroxene is locally rimmed by a green amphibole, the development of which increases in proximity to myrmekite and quartz development. Structure developed in association with oblique motions on the dextral, strike-slip Finlay-Ingenika fault (FIF) in the McConnell Creek area, north-central British Columbia, is dominated by subvertical to vertical strike-slip faults. characteristics of the region and describe the paleomagnetism of the plutonic rocks there. Finally, we describe how structural analysis may be used to correct discordant paleomagnetic directions. Tectonic Setting and Major Structures The study area lies within the eastern part of the Inter- montane Belt in north-central British Columbia (Figure 1) and straddles the boundary between the Quesnellia and Stikinia tectonostratigraphic terranes [Monger, 1984]. Stikinia, Cache Creek, Quesnellia, and Slide Mountain terranes had been essentially amalgamated by the Early Jurassic due to the closing of the Cache Creek ocean, forming the composite Terrane I, and were subsequently accreted to the ancient margin of North America during Middle Jurassic contraction [Monger, 1984]. Transcurrent motions between the Inter- montane Belt and North American craton occurred in the Late Cretaceous to Eocene at a time when the Kula plate in the west was converging obliquely with the North American plate [Engebretson et al., 1985; Umhoefer, 1987]. These motions apparently have produced dextral strike-slip displacements along the Tintina trench and northern Rocky Mountain trench (TT-NRMT) fault zone [Roddick, 1967; Tempelman-Kluit, 1979; Gabrielse, 1985; Struik, 1993] and a sequence of fa

ip faults trending east-northeast (Figure 2), as well as some large-scale northwest to north-northwest trending folds. Based on their geometric and spatial relationships, all these faults can be related to the stress field associated with movement on the FIF [Zhang and Hynes, 1994]. Strain analysis of the deformed volcanic fragments along one of the north-northwest trending, dextral strike-slip faults shows that the principal orientations of the strain ellipsoids are in accordance with those of the magnetic susceptibility ellipsoids from the adjacent deformed dioritic rocks, indicating that the plutonic rocks experienced the same deformation as the Late Triassic Takla Group volcanics [Zhang and Hynes, 1994]. The dextral displacement of --110 km along the FIF probably took place during middle Cretaceous or Late Cretaceous time, based on its crosscutting relationship with the Kutcho and Pinchi faults [Gabrielse, 1985]. The strike- slip faulting in the study area may therefore not have been earlier than middle Cretaceous as Early Jurassic to Cretaceous dioritic rocks were involved in the faulting in many places. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Mesozoic rocks from the Sierra de Los Organos and Sierra del Rosario fold belts of western Cuba revealed postfolding magnetisation in diabases of the Late Jurassic E1 SAbalo Formation and carbonates of the middle Cretaceous Pons and the Late Cretaceous Carmita and Moreno formations. Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. We rule out a possibility to account for these results by either horizontal movements or non-dipole field anomaly. Neither very appealing is a hypothesis of a post-remagnetization tilt of the entire region. All the components appear to be confined to a plane perpendicular to the main structural trends; we hypothesize that the remanences might have been distorted or re-aligned during deformation; this assumption, however, is far from being proven. In contrast, well-defined characteristic components were isolated from basaits of the Aptian-Albian Encrucijada (D/I = 2470/23 °, K= 14, a95 z 9.0 °) and the Late Cretaceous Orozco (D/l= 2280/22 °, K= 110, a95 = 4.7) formations from the Bahia Honda zone in the north of western Cuba; the remanence in the Encrucijada Formation is shown to predate deformation. Mean inclinations in both formations match those in Cretaceous volcanics from central Cuba, and all the results show lower latitudes than expected from the reference data

Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. We rule out a possibility to account for these results by either horizontal movements or non-dipole field anomaly. Neither very appealing is a hypothesis of a post-remagnetization tilt of the entire region. All the components appear to be confined to a plane perpendicular to the main structural trends; we hypothesize that the remanences might have been distorted or re-aligned during deformation; this assumption, however, is far from being proven. carrier_significance_candidates.excerpt: Mesozoic rocks from the Sierra de Los Organos and Sierra del Rosario fold belts of western Cuba revealed postfolding magnetisation in diabases of the Late Jurassic E1 SAbalo Formation and carbonates of the middle Cretaceous Pons and the Late Cretaceous Carmita and Moreno formations. All the components appear to be confined to a plane perpendicular to the main structural trends; we hypothesize that the remanences might have been distorted or re-aligned during deformation; this assumption, however, is far from being proven. E1 SAbalo Formation and carbonates of the middle Cretaceous Pons and the Late Cretaceous Carmita and Moreno formations. Steep components with inclinations of about 70 ° were isolated from all three formations; at the same time, postfolding shallow components were also found in a few samples of the Pons limestones. We rule out a possibility to account for these results by either horizontal movements or non-dipole field anomaly. Such a pattern, however, has never been observed either in the field or laboratory experiments (Klig- field et al., 1983; Cogne and Perroud, 1987). The strain hypothesis, however, infers strong internal de- formation, but neither cleavage nor other types of internal deformation were observed in either forma- tion. Besides, any internal deformation could hardly be so uniform as to result in close agreement of paleomagnetic directions from the sections about 100 km apart. Anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility might have been of help for testing the strain hypothesis; unfortunately, these sediments are very weakly mag- netized, and AMS measurements could not be per- formed. Nevertheless, the hypothesis that observed pattern of paleomagnetic directions is related to the deformational process cannot now be discarded. In principle, it is possible that the studied forma- tions were tilted after thrusting and folding and acquisition of remanence because the precise posi- tion of a rock mass with respect to the paleohorizon- tal is unknown for a postfolding component. A total of 61 sites (more than 700 cores) have been sampled mainly from limestones (Zongshan Formation, Jidula Formation Member II, Zongpu Formation), sandstones (Jidula Formation Member III) and graywackes (Gamba Group Member II), with ages well defined from detailed lithological and biostratigraphic analyses. The initial collision occurred in the western part with progressive closure of the Neo-Tethyan ocean from west to east (Klootwijk et al., 1985). Further conver- gence led to straightforward and rotational under- thrusting of the Indian Plate beneath the southern Eurasian margin since the Miocene. During the past years an earlier age for the collision has been pro- posed. Based on a review of primary and secondary palaeoremanences from the Himalaya and Hin- dukush and results from the Ninetyeast Ridge, Klootwijk et al. (1991, 1992) concluded that initial contact between India and Eurasia was already estab- lished at the Cretaceous/Tertiary time boundary. They interpret the drop in drift rate at 55-50 Ma as completion of closure of the Neo-Tethys. Occurrence of high-pressure rocks of eclogite facies in the Upper Kaghan Valley (northwestern Himalaya) with a peak metamorphic age of 49_ 6 Ma (Tonarini et al., 1993; Spencer, 1993) supports the hypothesis of an initial collision as early as 65 Ma in the western part. The study of Julien and Goff~ (1993) in the eastern Dauphinoise zone, for example, has demon- strated the existence of cooke'ite in Aalenian black shales. The occurrence of cooke'ite allows us to estimate the maximum temperature for the metamor- phism at around 325°C. The pressure estimated from fluid inclusion studies (Bernard, 1978; Jenatton, 1981; Nziengui, 1993) is around 200 MPa. This metamorphism is dated at around 26.5 Ma by Nzien- gui (1993). Thus the NRM carried by extremely stable fine-grained, probably single domain, pyrrhotite (Rochette and Lamarche, 1986 and Ro- chette et al., 1990) with a Curie temperature between 310°C and 335°C (Fig. 2a), is probably a thermore- manent magnetization (TRM) acquired during post metamorphic cooling. The occurence of antipodal normal and reverse polarities as a function of the altitude especialy in area 1 and 2 (Table 1), supports this interpretation. Moreover, the study of Rochette et al. (1992) in the same black schist facies but in the northern valley of Maurienne has shown the record of successive normal and reverse components versus temperature in the same sample, therefore strongly supporting our contention that NRM is a TRM. Even if a metamorphic CRM (chemical remanent magneti- za

ion) was responsible for our NRM, the directional interpretation would be identical. 3. Sampling and measurement We sampled 310 oriented cores in 44 sites from the Bourg d'Oisans area (Fig. 1), where the Liassic marly limestone facies is very well exposed. For each site we cored between 5 and 14 samples with a portable drill and oriented them with a magnetic compass. Local structural measurements were taken, in order to make corrections for bedding (SO) and cleavage (S 1). NRM measurements were carried out with a Mol- spin spinner magnetometer initially and after treat- ment at 150°C. For 1 or 2 specimens per site a progressive thermal demagnetization up to 350°C was carried out with the use of a CTF cryogenic magnetometer. The furnace used was a Pyrox fabri- cation and allowed us to heat 30 to 40 specimens in the same time. The residual field inside was less than about 10 nT. The susceptibility was measured using MS2 Bartington, after each heating step. Results from 5 sites with very low intensity of magnetization (< 0.05 mA/m), have not been taken into account in this study. Site mean directions for the characteris- tic remanent magnetization (ChRM) were deter- mined through Fisher (1953) statistics on the direc- tion remaining after demagnetization at 150°C (Table 1). The Zijderveld (1967) plots show the demagnetization of a single component during the thermal demagnetization between 150 ° and 325°C. Thus we can conclude that no significant motion occurred during cooling from 325 ° to 150 ° , and that the tilting must have occurred after cooling below 150°C. Cooling curves deduced from geochronologi- cal data in the Mont Blanc area (Soom, 1990) sug- gest a cooling rate of 10°/Ma. The age of the cooling below the 150 ° isotherm can thus be esti- mated at about 9-13 Ma. This is probably the oldest age possible for the tiltings. Introduction Characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) of late metamorphic age, can be used as a tectonic marker of the late history of a collision belt. In the Western Alps, the discovery of such a paleomagnetic signal carried by pyrrhotite (Rochette and Lamarche, 1986; Lamarche et al., 1988) allows us to test the existence of rotations around vertical or horizontal axes which occured after the cooling of these rocks. The magnetization clearly postdates the folds and so the main cleavage (S1 called $2 in Gratier et al., 1973). This penetrative deformation occurs during the late Oligocene. Tak- ing into account the age constraints on metamor- phism and tectonic phases, we can propose an age for remanence acquisition. If NRM is in fact a TRM, it dates from the post-metamorphic cooling, so we can suggest it began at about the Oligo-Miocene time boundary. Received 1995 August 30; in original form 1995 February 24 SUMMARY We present the magnetostratigraphy of the early Palaeozoic Moyero river section in north-western Siberia. The section investigated, which consists mainly of reddish limestones, mark and greyish limestones, extends from the upper Cambrian to the lower Silurian. Palaeomagnetic analyses reveal two magnetic components. One is interpreted as a remagnetization acquired during Siberian trap emplacement; the other is believed to be early diagenetic, consistent with the established lower Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path for Siberia. Reversed polarity dominates from the upper Cambrian to the middle Ordovician, while normal polarity dominates from the upper Ordovician to the lower Silurian. Only a few reversals, which are poorly defined, are observed through the section, in particular during the Llandeilo. These data are in agreement with previous magnetostratigraphic data from the Baltic platform and Siberia and indicate that magnetic reversal frequency was low during the Ordovician.

Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2). A detailed stratigraphic and bio- stratigraphic description of these exposures has been made by Mjagkova et al. (1963, 1977; in Russian) and Kanygin, Moscalenko & Yadrenkina (1987; in English). The Moyero region, as all of the Siberian platform, was an epicontinental sedimentation zone during the early Palaeozoic. The biostratigraphic data, based on conodonts and some macrofossils (e.g. brachiopods and cephalopods), indicate that 12 Ordovician stratigraphic horizons are present in the Moyero composite section, making it one of the best Ordovician sections from Eurasia in terms of dating and stratigraphic completeness (Kanygin et u1. 1987). However, a large strati- graphic gap is observed at the Ordovician/Silurian boundary. This hiatus is linked to the major oceanic regression that occurred during the uppermost Ordovician. In Moyero, this regression is marked by altered rocks indicating an emersion (and erosion) of long duration. The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2). A detailed stratigraphic and bio- stratigraphic description of these exposures has been made by Mjagkova et al. (1963, 1977; in Russian) and Kanygin, Moscalenko & Yadrenkina (1987; in English). The Moyero region, as all of the Siberian platform, was an epicontinental sedimentation zone during the early Palaeozoic. The biostratigraphic data, based on conodonts and some macrofossils (e.g. brachiopods and cephalopods), indicate that 12 Ordovician stratigraphic horizons are present in the Moyero composite section, making it one of the best Ordovician sections from Eurasia in terms of dating and stratigraphic completeness (Kanygin et u1. 1987). However, a large strati- graphic gap is observed at the Ordovician/Silurian boundary. This hiatus is linked to the major oceanic regression that occurred during the uppermost Ordovician. In Moyero, this regression is marked by altered rocks indicating an emersion (and erosion) of long duration. The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2). A detailed stratigraphic and bio- stratigraphic description of these exposures has been made by Mjagkova et al. (1963, 1977; in Russian) and Kanygin, Moscalenko & Yadrenkina (1987; in English). The Moyero region, as all of the Siberian platform, was an epicontinental sedimentation zone during the early Palaeozoic. The biostratigraphic data, based on conodonts and some macrofossils (e.g. brachiopods and cephalopods), indicate that 12 Ordovician stratigraphic horizons are present in the Moyero composite section, making it one of the best Ordovician sections from Eurasia in terms of dating and stratigraphic completeness (Kanygin et u1. 1987). In Moyero, this regression is marked by altered rocks indicating an emersion (and erosion) of long duration. The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2). The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Received 1995 August 30; in original form 1995 February 24 SUMMARY We present the magnetostratigraphy of the early Palaeozoic Moyero river section in north-western Siberia. The section investigated, which consists mainly of reddish limestones, mark and greyish limestones, extends from the upper Cambrian to the lower Silurian. Palaeomagnetic analyses reveal two magnetic components. One is interpreted as a remagnetization acquired during Siberian trap emplacement; the other is believed to be early diagenetic, consistent with the established lower Palaeozoic apparent polar wander path for Siberia. Reversed polarity dominates from the upper Cambrian to the middle Ordovician, while normal polarity dominates from the upper Ordovician to the lower Silurian. Only a few reversals, which are poorly defined, are observed through the section, in particular during the Llandeilo. These data are in agreement with previous magnetostratigraphic data from the Baltic platform and Siberia and indicate that magnetic reversal frequency was low during the Ordovician.

traps and the Deccan traps may be the traces of these plumes in the lithosphere, involving major biological crises at the Permo-Triassic and Cretaceous-Tertiary bound- aries, respectively (Courtillot & Besse 1987; Courtillot 1990). The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2). traps and the Deccan traps may be the traces of these plumes in the lithosphere, involving major biological crises at the Permo-Triassic and Cretaceous-Tertiary bound- aries, respectively (Courtillot & Besse 1987; Courtillot 1990). A detailed stratigraphic and bio- stratigraphic description of these exposures has been made by Mjagkova et al. (1963, 1977; in Russian) and Kanygin, Moscalenko & Yadrenkina (1987; in English). The Moyero region, as all of the Siberian platform, was an epicontinental sedimentation zone during the early Palaeozoic. The biostratigraphic data, based on conodonts and some macrofossils (e.g. brachiopods and cephalopods), indicate that 12 Ordovician stratigraphic horizons are present in the Moyero composite section, making it one of the best Ordovician sections from Eurasia in terms of dating and stratigraphic completeness (Kanygin et u1. 1987). However, a large strati- graphic gap is observed at the Ordovician/Silurian boundary. This hiatus is linked to the major oceanic regression that occurred during the uppermost Ordovician. In Moyero, this regression is marked by altered rocks indicating an emersion (and erosion) of long duration. The biostratigraphic data show that a record of the second half of the upper Ordovician and the lowermost Silurian is missing. Other sedimentary gaps probably exist within the Ordovician series, for example at the Llanvirn/Llandeilo boundary, but they seem to be of limited duration (Mjagkova et al. 1963, 1977). The Moyero river is located near the Siberian traps, which were dated recently at around 250Ma, close to the Permo- Triassic boundary (Claoue-Long et al. 1991; Renne & Basu 1991). Traces of these traps are observed in some exposures of the Moyero section, in the form of sills or dykes, which vary in thickness and lateral extent from decimetres to kilometres. In particular, the outcrops of Tremadoc age (lower Ordovician) are widely intruded by the traps. The sampled strata dip gently, on the order of 2-3", to the south-west. The northward flowing Moyero river cuts these strata and exposes successively Silurian to Cambrian levels (Fig. 1). Small oriented blocks were collected from 12 sections among the sites already listed and numbered by Mjagkova et ul. (1963, 1977; Fig. 2). A stable remanent magnetization is only found in the Asphaltkalk deposits, not in non-bitumen-impregnated limestones of the same age. The stable remanence was acquired after folding in this region, as revealed by a palaeomagnetic fold test. The timing of remanence acquisition is Late Cretaceous-early Tertiary, as derived from a comparison of the mean pole of the magnetic component with the European apparent polar wander path (APWP). The decay pattern of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) during alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetizaton indicates that the magnetization is carried by magnetite. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition and thermal decay measurements, as well as hysteresis parameters, are consistent with this interpretation. This study suggests that the creation of authigenic magnetite during the lower Tertiary in the Asphaltkalk deposits might coincide with the timing of hydrocarbon migration into the unit. Key words: Asphaltkalk, chemical remanent magnetization, magnetite. INTRODUCTION Many studies have shown a link between hydrocarbon migration and magnetization in limestones (e.g. Elmore et al. 1987; McCabe, Sassen & Saffer 1987; Kilgore & Elmore 1989; Reynolds et al. 1990). It is believed that the geochemical conditions produced by hydrocarbon migration can cause the creation of authigenic magnetic phases (e.g. Elmore et al. 1993; Machel 1995). This relationship can be used as a means of dating hydrocarbon migration events by deriving the timing of remanence acquisition from palaeomagnetic investigations. In this study we report palaeomagnetic and rock magnetic results from bitumen-impregnated limestones in northern Germany. We present evidence for the connection between hydrocarbon migration and the acquisition of a remanent magnetization. Furthermore, we attempt to date the migration event by resolving the age of the magnetization. PALAEOMAGNETIC PROPERTIES Samples were collected with a portable water-cooled rock drill and oriented with a magnetic compass. Sections KqA and KqB were sampled at an average sampling interval of 20-25 cm, with slightly coarser sampling (40-50 cm) at KqC. Each 2.5 cm diameter core sample yielded one and occasionally two standard llcc specimens, giving a total of 206 specimens for analysis. Thermal demagnetization treatments and measure- ments of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) were per- formed in a shielded room (where the ambient magnetic field was less than 300 mT). Heating and cooling were carried out in a well-shielded demagnetizer in which ambient fields were less than 5 nT. Magnetic remanences were measured with a 2G Model 760 three-axis cryogenic magnetometer. After each thermal demagnetization step, the initial magnetic suscept- ibility of each specimen was measured with a Bartington MS2 susceptibility bridge to monitor any mineralogical alteration resulting from the heating procedure. Least-squares analysis (Kirschvink 1980) was used to determine the component directions of NRM, chosen by inspection of vector end-point demagnetograms (Zijderveld 1967). Mean directions were determined with standard Fisher statistics.

riginal form 1996 March 26 SUMMARY Magnetobiostratigraphic data are presented from three Early/Middle Triassic Han- Bulog Limestone successions from Kqira, northern Albania. A total of 206 standard palaeomagnetic samples were obtained for thermal demagnetization and statistical analysis from the 42, 10 and 5m thick sections. The reversal-bearing characteristic component, carried by haematite and magnetite, defines a composite sequence of six main polarity intervals (Kqln to Kq3r) in which are embedded four short polarity intervals, one at the base of Kqln and three towards the top of Kqlr. The early acquisition of the characteristic remanence is supported by the lateral correlation of magnetozones between sections. The Early/Middle Triassic boundary, approximated by the first occurrence of the conodont Chiosella timorensis, falls close to the Kqlr/Kq2n polarity transition. This is in good agreement with recently published magneto- biostratigraphic data from the coeval Chios (Greece) sections. The palaeomagnetic pole calculated from the Kqira characteristic directions lies close to the Triassic portion of the apparent polar wander path for Laurussia (in European coordinates). However, a 40-45" clockwise rotation of the external zone of the Albano-Hellenic Belt to the south

Kqira area was evidently associated with West Gondwana and located at 12-16"N of the western Tethys margin. Key words: Albania, biostratigraphy, magnetostratigraphy, Triassic. INTRODUCTION Significant progress has been made in recent years in con- structing a Triassic geomagnetic polarity sequence correlated with biostratigraphic and chronostratigraphic data in Tethyan marine sections (e.g. Gallet et al. 1992, 1993, 1994; Muttoni et al. 1994; Graziano & Ogg 1994; Muttoni, Kent & Gaetani 1995). A polarity sequence across the Early/Middle Triassic boundary was recently obtained from the ammonoid- and conodont-bearing Marmarotrapeza Formation on Chios, Greece (Muttoni et al. 1995). However, the fossiliferous Tethyan limestone sections are often condensed and replication is needed to be sure that the magneto- and biostratigraphic representation is complete. We were able to obtain a magnetostratigraphic framework for the vertical distribution of ammonoids, conodonts and benthic foraminiferas. The boundary between them is drawn along the Darvaz-Karakul Fault [17], separating Mesozoic- Cenozoic rocks of the External zone from Paleozoic rocks of the North Pamir zone. Stratigraphic con- tacts, however, were locally found between Meso- zoic and Paleozoic rocks [18], and the Darvaz- Karakul Fault is probably a younger feature. At locality 1 in the Zaalay Range (Fig. lb), the Permian sequence, separated by a fault from Lower Carboniferous volcanics, comprises Lower Permian flysch and about 500 m thick light-coloured lime- stones, which are conformably overlain by violet and green sandstones and siltstones with some limestone layers (Gundara Formation). The boundary between them is drawn along the Darvaz-Karakul Fault [17], separating Mesozoic- Cenozoic rocks of the External zone from Paleozoic rocks of the North Pamir zone. Stratigraphic con- tacts, however, were locally found between Meso- zoic and Paleozoic rocks [18], and the Darvaz- Karakul Fault is probably a younger feature. At locality 1 in the Zaalay Range (Fig. lb), the Permian sequence, separated by a fault from Lower Carboniferous volcanics, comprises Lower Permian flysch and about 500 m thick light-coloured lime- stones, which are conformably overlain by violet and green sandstones and siltstones with some limestone layers (Gundara Formation). The counterparts of this formation to the west are of the early Late (Ufimian, c. 265 Ma) Permian age [19]. The Gundara rocks are overlain with erosional and probably weak angular unconformity by Late Permian conglomerates. With erosional disconformity, these conglomerates are overlain by a more than 2,000 m thick sequence of elastics, lava and tuffs of the Late Triassic-Early Jurassic Minteke Formation, metamorphosed to greenstone facies. The Gundara rocks are overlain with erosional and probably weak angular unconformity by Late Permian conglomerates. UK Received 23 February 1996; accepted 3 June 1996 Abstract The Aegean region is characterised by major fault-bound blocks with markedly contrasting structural trends. Recent models account for these variations either through differential block rotation or through a process of radial extension. The Cycladic Massif in the back-arc region to the Hellenic trench represents a critical area where apparently divergent extension directions are observed. This contribution provides the first palaeomagnetic results from this area. Magnetic remanence and AMS data are presented for Middle Miocene granodiorites on the islands of Mykonos and Naxos. These rocks are exposed in the footwalls of major extensional detachments within the metamorphic core complexes that characterise the Cycladic Massif. A clear correlation between the orientation of an L-S fabric developed within the intrusions and the magnetic fabric data is observed, demonstrating the presence of a ‘normal’ magnetic fabric of extensional origin. The mean extension directions inferred from the orientations of the maximum axes of the magnetic susceptibility ellipsoids are markedly divergent at 064” (Mykonos) and 35 1” (Naxos). North

n situ magnetisations back to the reference direction may be found by consideration of regional structural trends, assuming that tilting is controlled by the major block-bounding faults. These solutions indicate significant components of differential vertical axis rotations across the Cyclades. Mykonos is bound by NW-SE trending regional faults and is shown to have rotated clockwise by ca. 22”. In contrast, Naxos is bound by ENE-WSW trending structures and has rotated anticlockwise by ca. 33”. The apparent divergence of extension directions inferred from both the magnetic anisotropy and structural data is resolved by correcting the mean AMS data for subsequent rotation using the rotation solutions derived from the magnetic remanence data. The data imply that the primary Middle Miocene extension direction in the Cycladic Massif was nearly uniform along a NNE-SSW azimuth. The Cycladic Massif in the back-arc region to the Hellenic trench represents a critical area where apparently divergent extension directions are observed. These rocks are exposed in the footwalls of major extensional detachments within the metamorphic core complexes that characterise the Cycladic Massif. These solutions indicate significant components of differential vertical axis rotations across the Cyclades. Mykonos is bound by NW-SE trending regional faults and is shown to have rotated clockwise by ca. 22”. In contrast, Naxos is bound by ENE-WSW trending structures and has rotated anticlockwise by ca. 33”. The apparent divergence of extension directions inferred from both the magnetic anisotropy and structural data is resolved by correcting the mean AMS data for subsequent rotation using the rotation solutions derived from the magnetic remanence data. UK Received 23 February 1996; accepted 3 June 1996 Abstract The Aegean region is characterised by major fault-bound blocks with markedly contrasting structural trends. Recent models account for these variations either through differential block rotation or through a process of radial extension. The Cycladic Massif in the back-arc region to the Hellenic trench represents a critical area where apparently divergent extension directions are observed. This contribution provides the first palaeomagnetic results from this area. Magnetic remanence and AMS data are presented for Middle Miocene granodiorites on the islands of Mykonos and Naxos. These rocks are exposed in the footwalls of major extensional detachments within the metamorphic core complexes that characterise the Cycladic Massif. A clear correlation between the orientation of an L-S fabric developed within the intrusions and the magnetic fabric data is observed, demonstrating the presence of a ‘normal’ magnetic fabric of extensional origin. These rocks are exposed in the footwalls of major extensional detachments within the metamorphic core complexes that characterise the Cycladic Massif. A clear correlation between the orientation of an L-S fabric developed within the intrusions and the magnetic fabric data is observed, demonstrating the presence of a ‘normal’ magnetic fabric of extensional origin. A third hypothesis of ‘erogenic fluids’ driven through a large mass of rock as a result of continental collision [22] is very popu- lar and frequently invoked. However, direct link between such fluids and the remagnetization event has not been made [23] and the viability and driving force for regional fluid migration on such a large scale are still questionable [24]. As for the carbonate rocks investigated in this study, the cause(s) for the remagnetization is difficult to ascertain without fur- ther petrological and rock magnetic analyses. Weath- ering is probably the dominant factor responsible for the Cenozoic overprint of the Longtou and Huaxi formations because the age of the remagnetization has been demonstrated to be very recent and the major magnetic carrier is hematite with a possible goethitic precursor. The origin of magnetite in these two formations is unclear, and it may be a product of dolomitization, such as that observed by Hart and Fuller [25] in a Cenozoic dolomite bed, but this would require that the dolomitization take place in very recent times. Instead, severe late Cretaceous to Recent remagnetizations have been revealed from all the three rock formations studied. In all cases, the in situ characteristic remanent magnetization (ChRM) directions resemble or fall close to the local present-day Earth’s magnetic field direction and fail the fold test, despite the presence of dual polarity in two formations. The major magnetic carriers of the remagnetizations are hematite and magnetite. The cause(s) for the remagnetization events cannot be ascertained at present, but weathering in recent time and migrating fluid in the past might be responsible. The tilt-corrected ChRM direction from Puxi is congruent with those from Badong and Sangzhi but is based on a smaller number of samples collected from a monocline. These ChRM directions are believed to be primary. The data indicates that Badong has been rotated clockwise by 13.6 + 8.5” relative to Sangzhi, which, in turn, has possibly been rotated in the same sense with respect to other parts of the Yangtze Block (YB) except eastern Sichuan based on the bend of the sampled fold axis and the Lower Triassic paleomagnetic data published for the YB. The Lower and Middle Triassic paleomagnetic data together appear to indicate that eastern Sichuan and the border area between Sichuan, Guizhou, Hubei and Hunan provinces have been affected by differential rotations, probably due to oroclinal bending. The paleomagnetic data obtained from this study further constrain the timing of the final suturing of the YB with the North China Block (NCB) to be post-Middle Triassic. A 210 m section of Late Triassic Fleming Fjord Formation (the Malmros Klint Member and the lowermost 80m of the overlying Carlsberg Fjord beds of the Ørsted Dal Member) in the Tait Bjerg area of the Jameson Land Basin, East Greenland, was sampled for paleomagnetic study and measured for cycle stratigraphie analysis. Paleomagnetic samples were also taken from the underlying Gipsdalen Formation in the Gipsdalen area. A high stability character- istic magnetization carried by hematite was successfully isolated in 63 sampling levels in the Fleming Fjord Formation and 9 sampling sites in the Gipsdalen Formation using pro- gressive thermal demagnetization. The mean characteristic directions for the Herning Fjord and the Gipsdalen Formations may be be biased by sedimentary inclination error but are consistent with a northward drift of East Greenland of about 10° from the arid (ca. 25° N) to semihumid (ca. 35° N) paleoclimatic belts in the Middle to Late Triassic. Seven normal and reversed polarity intervals are clearly delineated in the Fleming Fjord Formation section. Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Forma- tions may be due to a sedimentary inclination error pro- duced during or shortly after deposition. Inclination error is the difference between expected (Ie) and ob- served (Io) inclinations which are related as: f=tan(Io)/ tan(Ie) for detrital rémanent magnetizations (King, 1955). The flattening factor, f, can range from 0 (com- plete shallowing) to 1 (no shallowing). The presence of a systematic inclination error in ancient red beds has long been disputed but generally thought to be unim- portant (e.g., Irving, 1967; Créer, 1967; Van derVoo et al., 1995). However, detrital rémanent magnetization carried by hematite in laboratory redeposition experi- ments as well as in some modern natural deposits has been associated with an inclination error characterized by f values of about 0.5 for ambient field inclinations up to 60° (Tauxe & Kent, 1984; Lovlie &Torsvik, 1984). For the Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Formations, the flattening factor would need to be only about 0.6 if incli- nation error was responsible for the anomalously shal- low directions. A 210 m section of Late Triassic Fleming Fjord Formation (the Malmros Klint Member and the lowermost 80m of the overlying Carlsberg Fjord beds of the Ørsted Dal Member) in the Tait Bjerg area of the Jameson Land Basin, East Greenland, was sampled for paleomagnetic study and measured for cycle stratigraphie analysis. Paleomagnetic samples were also taken from the underlying Gipsdalen Formation in the Gipsdalen area. A high stability character- istic magnetization carried by hematite was successfully isolated in 63 sampling levels in the Fleming Fjord Formation and 9 sampling sites in the Gipsdalen Formation using pro- gressive thermal demagnetization. The mean characteristic directions for the Herning Fjord and the Gipsdalen Formations may be be biased by sedimentary inclination error but are consistent with a northward drift of East Greenland of about 10° from the arid (ca. 25° N) to semihumid (ca. 35° N) paleoclimatic belts in the Middle to Late Triassic. Seven normal and reversed polarity intervals are clearly delineated in the Fleming Fjord Formation section. Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Forma- tions may be due to a sedimentary inclination error pro- duced during or shortly after deposition. Inclination error is the difference between expected (Ie) and ob- served (Io) inclinations which are related as: f=tan(Io)/ tan(Ie) for detrital rémanent magnetizations (King, 1955). The flattening factor, f, can range from 0 (com- plete shallowing) to 1 (no shallowing). The presence of a systematic inclination error in ancient red beds has long been disputed but generally thought to be unim- portant (e.g., Irving, 1967; Créer, 1967; Van derVoo et al., 1995). However, detrital rémanent magnetization carried by hematite in laboratory redeposition experi- ments as well as in some modern natural deposits has been associated with an inclination error characterized by f values of about 0.5 for ambient field inclinations up to 60° (Tauxe & Kent, 1984; Lovlie &Torsvik, 1984). For the Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Formations, the flattening factor would need to be only about 0.6 if incli- nation error was responsible for the anomalously shal- low directions. The reddish color of the sampled Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen sediments and the high maximum unblock- ing temperatures of their NRM point to hematite as the principal magnetic mineral. Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Forma- tions may be due to a sedimentary inclination error pro- duced during or shortly after deposition. Inclination error is the difference between expected (Ie) and ob- served (Io) inclinations which are related as: f=tan(Io)/ tan(Ie) for detrital rémanent magnetizations (King, 1955). The flattening factor, f, can range from 0 (com- plete shallowing) to 1 (no shallowing). The presence of a systematic inclination error in ancient red beds has long been disputed but generally thought to be unim- portant (e.g., Irving, 1967; Créer, 1967; Van derVoo et al., 1995). However, detrital rémanent magnetization carried by hematite in laboratory redeposition experi- ments as well as in some modern natural deposits has been associated with an inclination error characterized by f values of about 0.5 for ambient field inclinations up to 60° (Tauxe & Kent, 1984; Lovlie &Torsvik, 1984). For the Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Formations, the flattening factor would need to be only about 0.6 if incli- nation error was responsible for the anomalously shal- low directions. Inclination error is the difference between expected (Ie) and ob- served (Io) inclinations which are related as: f=tan(Io)/ tan(Ie) for detrital rémanent magnetizations (King, 1955). The flattening factor, f, can range from 0 (com- plete shallowing) to 1 (no shallowing). The presence of a systematic inclination error in ancient red beds has long been disputed but generally thought to be unim- portant (e.g., Irving, 1967; Créer, 1967; Van derVoo et al., 1995). However, detrital rémanent magnetization carried by hematite in laboratory redeposition experi- ments as well as in some modern natural deposits has been associated with an inclination error characterized by f values of about 0.5 for ambient field inclinations up to 60° (Tauxe & Kent, 1984; Lovlie &Torsvik, 1984). For the Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen Formations, the flattening factor would need to be only about 0.6 if incli- nation error was responsible for the anomalously shal- low directions. The reddish color of the sampled Fleming Fjord and Gipsdalen sediments and the high maximum unblock- ing temperatures of their NRM point to hematite as the principal magnetic mineral. The longest, first-order cycles (duration >50 Ma) are regarded as tectono-eustatic in origin, i.e. caused by changes in the volume of the oceans due to plate-tectonic processes. The majority of the second-order (3-50 Ma) cycles are believed to be tec- tonically induced transgressive-regressive facies cycles. The third-order cycles (0.5-3 Ma) are bounded by major eustatic sea-level falls (the amplitude of sea-level change being a few tens of metres). The fourth- (0.08-0.5 Ma), fifth- (0.03-0.08 Ma) and sixth- order (0.01-0.03 Ma) cycles are within the frequency band of the orbitally forced Milankovitch climatic cycles. The ampli- tudes of the sea-level oscillations in this case are tens of metres in ‘ice-house’ periods and up to several metres in ‘green- house’ periods. As Goldhammer, Dunn & Hardie (1990) demonstrated, certain characteristics (e.g. thickness and facies) of a short-term cycle are controlled by longer-term (higher-order) sea-level variations due to changes in the accommodation depth. For instance, in the lowstand phase of the 3rd-order cycles, the 4th- to 6th-order cycles are probably condensed and dominated by subaerial facies and the subtidal facies are either very thin or totally absent. NTRODUCTION It is well known that carbonates have a weak natural remanent magnetization (NRM). Mesozoic carbonates, particularly shal- low-water facies, in the Mediterranean region are no exception: they often fail to yield any meaningful palaeomagnetic signal. Later, shallowing-upward cycles were also discovered in the Late Triassic Dolomia Principale of the Southern Alps (Bosellini 1965, 1967; Bosellini & Hardie 1985). Symmetric Lofer cycles (A-B-C-B) were first described from the Norian-Rhaetian Dachstein Limestone of the Bakony Mountains (Haas 1982, 1991). Schwarzacher & Haas (1986) referred to the Lofer cycles defined above as basic cycles and Strasser (1991), using the terminology of sequence stratigraphy, described them as small- scale depositional sequences. The longest, first-order cycles (duration >50 Ma) are regarded as tectono-eustatic in origin, i.e. caused by changes in the volume of the oceans due to plate-tectonic processes. The majority of the second-order (3-50 Ma) cycles are believed to be tec- tonically induced transgressive-regressive facies cycles. The third-order cycles (0.5-3 Ma) are bounded by major eustatic sea-level falls (the amplitude of sea-level change being a few tens of metres). The fourth- (0.08-0.5 Ma), fifth- (0.03-0.08 Ma) and sixth- order (0.01-0.03 Ma) cycles are within the frequency band of the orbitally forced Milankovitch climatic cycles. The ampli- tudes of the sea-level oscillations in this case are tens of metres in ‘ice-house’ periods and up to several metres in ‘green- house’ periods. As Goldhammer, Dunn & Hardie (1990) demonstrated, certain characteristics (e.g. thickness and facies) of a short-term cycle are controlled by longer-term (higher-order) sea-level variations due to changes in the accommodation depth. For instance, in the lowstand phase of the 3rd-order cycles, the 4th- to 6th-order cycles are probably condensed and dominated by subaerial facies and the subtidal facies are either very thin or totally absent. NTRODUCTION It is well known that carbonates have a weak natural remanent magnetization (NRM). Mesozoic carbonates, particularly shal- low-water facies, in the Mediterranean region are no exception: they often fail to yield any meaningful palaeomagnetic signal. Normally, a large number of samples must be studied, with the prospect of obtaining positive results from 40 to 50 per cent of these (e.g. Marton & Veljovic 1983, 1987; Marton & Pugliese 1989; Marton, Milicevic & Veljovic 1990; Marton & DAndrea 1992). In contrast, young platform and reefal carbonates seem to have preserved continuous records of the geomagnetic field. Thus, polarity zones can be determined in these rocks and magnetostratigraphy can be applied to a range of problems, such as the timing of atoll growth (Aissaoui, McNeill & Kirschvink 1990). Later, shallowing-upward cycles were also discovered in the Late Triassic Dolomia Principale of the Southern Alps (Bosellini 1965, 1967; Bosellini & Hardie 1985). Symmetric Lofer cycles (A-B-C-B) were first described from the Norian-Rhaetian Dachstein Limestone of the Bakony Mountains (Haas 1982, 1991). Haas suggested that this cycle type be regarded as standard, since all the observed stacking patterns can be derived from a symmetric cycle (Haas 1982). Schwarzacher & Haas (1986) referred to the Lofer cycles defined above as basic cycles and Strasser (1991), using the terminology of sequence stratigraphy, described them as small- scale depositional sequences. The most probable duration of a basic Lofer cycle is about 20 ka (Schwarzacher & Haas 1986), which corresponds to the shortest Milankovitch period. The Asturian-Cantabrian Arc (Fig. l), a foreland thrust- and-fold belt in the external part of the Variscan Belt in northwest Spain, forms the core of the Ibero-Armorican Arc. A large number of thrusts and folds can be observed, which define the form of the Arc. The relative ages and positions of synorogenic units permit the establishment of the ages of emplacement of the main thrust units. Although palaeomagnetism cannot a priori discriminate between the possible mechanisms by which oroclines form, the technique is well established as a powerful tool to constrain the kinematics of curvature or more simply to test whether any bending (is. rotations) occurred. The Sicilian-Calabrian, Umbrian, Central Appalachian, Wyoming-Idaho and Ibero-Armorican arcs are examples of oroclines that have been studied palaeo- magnetically (Eldredge, Bachtadse & Van der Voo 1985; Lowrie & Hirt 1986 and references therein). The Asturian-Cantabrian Arc (Fig. l), a foreland thrust- and-fold belt in the external part of the Variscan Belt in northwest Spain, forms the core of the Ibero-Armorican Arc. A large number of thrusts and folds can be observed, which define the form of the Arc. The relative ages and positions of synorogenic units permit the establishment of the ages of emplacement of the main thrust units. These stratigraphic data indicate that the allochtonous units of the Cantabrian zone were emplaced in Westphalian B to Stephanian ages. carrier_investigation_candidates.excerpt: of orogenic belts has been the topic of numerous palaeomagnetic studies ever since Carey (1955) first proposed the concept of ‘oroclines’ and oroclinal bending. Although palaeomagnetism cannot a priori discriminate between the possible mechanisms by which oroclines form, the technique is well established as a powerful tool to constrain the kinematics of curvature or more simply to test whether any bending (is. rotations) occurred. The Sicilian-Calabrian, Umbrian, Central Appalachian, Wyoming-Idaho and Ibero-Armorican arcs are examples of oroclines that have been studied palaeo- magnetically (Eldredge, Bachtadse & Van der Voo 1985; Lowrie & Hirt 1986 and references therein). The Asturian-Cantabrian Arc (Fig. l), a foreland thrust- and-fold belt in the external part of the Variscan Belt in northwest Spain, forms the core of the Ibero-Armorican Arc. A large number of thrusts and folds can be observed, which define the form of the Arc. The relative ages and positions of synorogenic units permit the establishment of the ages of emplacement of the main thrust units. These stratigraphic data indicate that the allochtonous units of the Cantabrian zone were emplaced in Westphalian B to Stephanian ages.
